nodes.question: How are mitigation and adaptation characterized in the context of this study?
nodes.answer: Mitigation and adaptation are characterized as public goods because they provide benefits to all countries.
nodes.paragraph: Abstract The purpose of the paper is to study how research and development (R&D) into adaptation technologies and mitigation activity for the reduction of emissions can influence participation in International Environmental Agreements (IEAs). Both mitigation and adaptation are supposed to be a public good because both produce the benefit of all countries. The model is employed in the context of non-coopera- tive dynamic games. Countries are involved in a two-stage game. In the first stage, each country decides upon its participation in the agreement, that means collec- tively deciding their mitigation and adaptation policies. In the second stage, coun- tries decide on their mitigation strategies and investment in R&D, either individu- ally or collectively, depending on their decision in the first stage. Members of the agreement fully share their knowledge about adaptation capacity and there is the assumption that some knowledge unintentionally spills over between a signatory and a non-signatory country and between two non-signatory countries. nodes.question: What do the studies by Lazkano et al. (2016) and others suggest about the nature of adaptation?
nodes.answer: They suggest that adaptation is primarily a private good, affecting only the welfare of the host country, although some studies imply it could also resemble a public good.
nodes.paragraph: While mitigation activity is always consid- ered as a public, international good, about adaptation, different scenarios have been proposed. In Lazkano et al. (2016), Rohrer and Rubio (2024) and Benchekroun et al. (2017) adaptation is a private good that only affects the welfare of the host coun- try instead (Masoudi & Zaccour 2017) and Masoudi and Zaccour (2018) assume that adaptation has a public good flavor. In Bayramoglu et al. (2018) it is studied the strategic interaction between mitigation (public good) and adaptation (private good) in a climate agreement. The view that adaptation is a private good is certainly correct when the focus is on the use of a specific adaptation technology. However, new knowledge about adaptation requires investments in research and development (R&D), which can be shared by different entities, with the resulting new technolo- gies benefiting all parties. All paper cited are modelled as a multi-stage game where players select their level of emissions and their level of adaptation in different stages and results indicate that the simultaneous deciding of adaptation and mitigation levels may have a positive effect on the stability of IEAs.

nodes.question: What is the novelty of the paper discussed in the provided text?
nodes.answer: The novelty lies in the coexistence of mitigation and adaptation, both considered to have public good characteristics.
nodes.paragraph: In Hongxiu and Rus (2019), authors consider a model based on simultaneous-move, where countries concomitantly choose their level of emissions/abatement and adaptation, instead in Finus et al. (2021) authors show, in a mitigation-adaptation game, that stable coalitions are larger in the Stackelberg than in the Nash-Cournot scenario, obtaining a generalization of Barrett S pure mitigation game. In this the paper, starting from Breton and Sbragia (2019), Baris and Zaccour (2018) and Masoudi and Zaccour (2018), we propose a two-stage coalition forma- tion game, where in the first stage countries decide whether or not to sign the agree- ment and in the second stage, signatories and defectors select their levels of miti- gation and adaptation in order to minimize their cost function. The novelty of the paper lies in the coexistence of mitigation and adaptation, both considered to have a public good flavor. In fact, following Breton & Sbragia (2019), we assume that miti- gation has public, international characteristics, while following Masoudi & Zaccour (2017) and Masoudi & Zaccour (2018), we assume that adaptation has a public good flavor and we study the impact of collective effort in R&D adaptation technologies.

nodes.question: Why are herbivores considered interesting organisms to study in the context of global change?
nodes.answer: Herbivores are interesting to study because they are sensitive to both direct and indirect effects of global change, such as alterations in host-plant quality or availability.

Both, eutrophication and climate change, likely play a significant role in biodiversity loss, specifically in the decline of insect diversity and abundance (Nessel et al. 2021; Raven and Wagner 2021). Herbivores comprise particularly interesting organisms to study the consequences of global change, as they are sensi- tive to direct as well as indirect effects, the latter being medi- ated by alterations in host-plant quality or availability (Har - vey et al. 2020; Kuczyk et al. 2021a). nodes.answer: Winning species are well adapted to human disturbance, while losing species are poorly adapted to such changes.

nodes.question: What range of definitions exist for a healthy ecosystem?
nodes.answer: Definitions range from a sustainable ecosystem, modified by human intervention, that uses its vital functions to prosper and demonstrate resilience to stress, to those emphasizing human health analogies and ecological integrity.
nodes.paragraph: 1). The manifold health consequences, particularly disruption of social interactions and cohesion, emergence of infectious diseases and disease vectors, as well as intoxication events, have been widely studied to understand the evolution of the quality of life in human societies (e.g. Martinez-Juarez et al. 2015; Summers et al. 2012; Sandifer et al. 2015; Karr 2011). Despite the rich literature on the consequences of degraded or unhealthy ecosystems for human health, there is no consensus on a final definition of ecosystem health. Defini- tions of a healthy ecosystem range from a sustainable ecosystem, modified and impacted by human intervention, that uses its vital functions to prosper and is resilient to stress (Cos- tanza and Mageau 1999) to definitions revolving around human health analogies, or eco- logical integrity (Lackey 2001; Scrimgeour and Wicklum 1996). The notion of ecosystem health is often used as a synonym of ecological integrity, despite their obvious differences (Karr and Chu 1995; Karr et al. 2020). Ecological integrity was described as the ability of an ecosystem to support and maintain diverse, balanced, integrated, and adaptive biological 725 Biodiversity and Conservation (2025) 34:723 767 communities and ecological processes in a stable state, combining physical, chemical, and biological integrity (Karr and Chu 1995).

nodes.question: Why is it difficult to define a natural or historical reference state of an ecosystem in the Anthropocene?
nodes.answer: It is difficult to define a natural or historical reference state of an ecosystem due to the dominance of human activities and the high degree of environmental alteration.
nodes.paragraph: Ecological integrity is considered to be meas- urable by comparing composition, structure, and function to natural or historic ranges of variation (Bridgewater et al. 2014). However, in the Anthropocene, it appears to be difficult to define a natural state or a historical reference state of an ecosystem due to the dominance of human activities and the high degree of environmental alteration (Hansen et al. 2021). The concept of ecosystem health does evaluate the condition of ecosystems, using diverse indicators of habitats, species, and resources, as well as indicators of function, allowing to assess if an ecosystem is able to retain natural functions and the capacity to deliver ecosys- tem services (Burkhard et al. 2008). The ecosystem health concept, in a decisive difference to ecological integrity, integrates environmental conditions with anthropogenic impacts to inform about the sustainable use and management of natural resources. Understanding both concepts, ecological integrity and ecosystem health, ask for a large amount of data on abiotic and biotic variables, which are often only available on local scales, but not at larger scales, an issue also addressed with the concepts of Essential Biodiversity Varia- bles (Haase et al.

nodes.question: How is TEK regarded in relation to environmental and climatic change?
nodes.answer: TEK is deemed a critical knowledge system for fostering adaptation and resilience to environmental and climatic change.
nodes.paragraph: Social capital refers to relationships and structures that make a given social unit more effective, and its theory has been exten- sively discussed in the last few decades (Putnam, 2000). Social capital is essential for sus- tainability because it facilitates cooperation and reciprocity among community members (Pretty & Smith, 2004). The significance of TEK worldwide is reflected in its inclusion in many global envi- ronmental governance fora. The World Heritage Convention of the United Nations Educa- tional, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) and the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) acknowledge the importance of TEK in achieving the global conservation agenda (see Fajardo et al., 2021; Aswani et al., 2018). TEK is deemed a critical knowl- edge system for fostering adaptation and resilience to environmental and climatic change (Cinner et al., 2018). TEK use is widespread, covering various contexts and settings (see Berkes, 2010; Berkes et al., 2000). TEK is further regarded as a crucial alternative and/ or complementary to traditionally acquired scientific data, particularly in highly complex environments and in data-poor contexts (see Johannes, 1998).

nodes.answer: The speed of morphological change must keep pace with the speed of environmental change; anthropogenic changes can occur extremely rapidly, making adaptation a real challenge.

Anthro - pogenic changes can be extremely rapid, making adapta - tion a real challenge (Jacobs et al. 2019 ). Human activity is transforming natural habitats into modified environments and intensifies land use at an ever-increasing rate. These land use changes include amongst others urbanisation and agriculture (Foley et al. 2005 ). Their consequences are numerous and have resulted in habitat fragmentation and deforestation ultimately leading to biodiversity loss (Defries et al. 2004 ). nodes.question: How do land-use and climate change influence ecosystem interactions?
nodes.answer: Land-use and climate change affect the interactions among various factors, resulting in changes in the intensity of their effects on ecosystems.

However, most current studies concentrate on recording the influence of climate and land-use changes on individuals or a few natural properties, overlooking the coupled interactions among socio-ecological elements, which may lead to an increased risk of uncertainty12,14,27 Social and ecological components are highly interrelated. Except for land-use and climate change, landscape patterns, geomorphological features, and other human activities also drive ecosystem services and functions12. However, these factors rarely operate independently and may interact in opposition or synergy28. Land-use and climate change affect the interactions among these factors, resulting in changes in the intensity of their effects on ecosystems. In addition, an increasing number of studies have highlighted that a continuous increase in pressure from land-use or climate changes may result in systematic and abrupt shifts in SES, thereby altering the relationships between SES components. For example, research in the arid regions of northern China shows that the relationship between plant and microbial diversity and soil multifunctionality shifts when aridity exceeds a threshold of 0.829.

nodes.question: Why is identifying the threshold in ecosystem responses important?
nodes.answer: Identifying and clarifying the existence of the threshold is fundamental to developing adaptive ecological management and planning strategies.
nodes.paragraph: Similarly, studies on forest and grassland ecosystems have found that increased land-use intensity causes a shift from trade-offs to weak synergistic relationships among biodiversity, ecosystem functions, and services30. Identifying and clarifying the existence of the threshold is fundamental to developing adaptive ecological management and planning strategies31. Regrettably, current research has been sparse in uncovering the interconnected dynamics of SES elements with land-use and climate change, particularly the threshold effects of such responses. The various nonlinear dynamic modeling techniques have paved the way for conceptualizing and visualizing SES. Agent-based models (ABM) and system dynamics (SD) are two traditional approaches for modeling SES, widely applied in complex systems such as grazing systems32, coral reefs33, forest management34, and coastal fisheries35. ABM can simulate the behavior and interactions of individual components within a system. However, it typically relies on explicitly defined connection rules between components. Moreover, computational costs increase significantly as the number of components grows. While SD models the complex dynamic changes of SES by determining causal relationships between components, it tends to focus more on macro-level feedback loops, often overlooking the micro-level heterogeneity of agents, and is less effective in simulating the system S response to sudden disturbances.

nodes.question: What are the key drivers of ecological status changes identified in the study?
nodes.answer: The key drivers identified are changes in abiotic stressors, biotic interactions (particularly interspecific competition), and land use.
nodes.paragraph: Abstract Background The global freshwater biodiversity crisis has led to widespread implementation of measures to counter - act environmental degradation and biodiversity loss. While these efforts aim to foster recovery, intensifying stressors continue to drive complex biotic responses, the trajectories and drivers of which are insufficiently understood. This study examines the roles of abiotic stressors, biotic interactions (e.g., competition), and land use in shaping ecological status changes across Germany, using data from 1599 river sites sampled at least twice between 2004 and 2022. Results Changes in abiotic stressors emerged as the most consistent drivers of ecological status, explaining sub - stantial variation (R2 = 0.39) and similar slopes for recovery ( = 0.11) and degradation ( = 0.10). Biotic interactions, particularly interspecific competition, also influenced the ecological status (R2 = 0.11), with stronger positive effects observed during recovery ( = 2.99) compared to degradation ( = 1.59). Land use effects varied by context: Streams in catchments with higher cropland or urban areas showed greater likelihood of recovery, whereas streams in forested catchments were more prone to degradation.

nodes.question: How are urban exploiters and adaptors defined in the context of the Australian urban environment?
nodes.answer: Urban exploiters are species that thrive in urban areas due to environmental modifications, while urban adaptors can survive in urban settings but are not as adept at exploiting the conditions; their persistence depends on the actions of urban residents.
nodes.paragraph: We present our commentary in two themes: (a) mitigating threats to birds in the urban environ- ment and (b) enhancing the habitat value of the urban environment for a broader range of bird species. In a new approach to this conversation, this paper brings together key topics that can no longer be considered in isolation if we are to make significant conservation gains in the environ- ments were most Australians now reside. Under climate warming scenarios, tree growth rates, and subsequently biomass accumulation and carbon stor - age, will be affected. However, the assessment of climate change effects on tree biomass is far from straightforward due to the difficulty in disentangling the effects of tem- poral climate change drivers from temporal endogenous processes (Chen and Luo 2015). The climate effects on ecosystem structure and functioning may be modified by interactions of soil, vegetation and hydrologic pat- terns with spatially variability of land use histories and human activities over a range of time scales (Groffman et al. 2012). Simulation models to explore the effects of climate change on European forest carbon cycles suggest a reduced efficiency of forests to absorb carbon in the future because of drought, heat stress and wildfires (Hale et al. 2019). Age-modulated growth response to climate has been suggested as a widespread phenomenon for different tree species growing under variable environmental condi- tions (Carrer and Urbinati 2004).
